content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper proposes a new approach for sound separation. It includes a semantic grouping network which learns category specific features from the audio which is then used to separate the output audio sources.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths: The paper's idea is interesting. I like that it is trying to provide more interpretability to source separation methods and and is explicitly modeling the underlying source categories. The paper is well written and easy to follow. All parts of the method are well motivated, and the figures and tables are very clear. The fact that the intermediate representation of the audio sources are well grouped and separated is a nice result. It can also handle a different number of sources than during training which is better than many audio-only separation networks that are trained for a specific number of output sources.

Weaknesses: Firstly, I don't like the framing of the paper in context of audio-visual methods. It's true that audio-visual methods use the video to learn a semantic understanding of sound, but audio only methods absolutely learn this semantic representation implicitly. This paper is just trying to be more explicit about the semantic understanding of source types and learning them in a more interpretable way. This method is not as closely related to audio-visual separation as the authors suggest. 

The method itself is a spectrogram based method that uses the binary masking approach to source separation. Such an approach has an upper bound in performance given by the ideal-ratio mask baseline. In recent years, time-domain approaches have appeared which have far surpassed this theoretic baseline of frequency masking approaches. The authors claim to be state-of-the-art, but time-domain separation methods like Demucs and SepFormer have not been compared even though such methods far outperform ideal frequency masking results. A quick look at Demucs shows that their output is around 7.7SDR on the MusDB dataset (4 way musical separation task) which is higher than the outputs here on the MUSIC dataset. Perhaps I missed something but it just doesn't make sense to me that a frequency masking approach can be state-of-the-art in a source separation task anymore. 

Finally, any source separation paper really needs to have qualitative examples for reviewers and readers in the supplementary materials. The baseline papers here (sound of pixels, Wave Unet etc) all have very thorough experimental results and real world examples. This allows the reader to understand the results qualitatively and how they compare to baseline results.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity - Very High
Novelty - Good idea for the explicit semantic grouping
Reproducibility - Well explained methods
Quality - Good quality paper
content.summary_of_the_review: Interesting idea, but framing and experiments need to be more thorough to account for the wide range of recent audio-only source separation networks. The paper is doing nice job of representation learning in this task, but I would need to see a few changes before recommending it for acceptance.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 4: The contributions are significant, and do not exist in prior works.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper:
This paper proposes an architecture called the "semantic grouping network (SGN)" for sound separation. First, a convoutional patch encoder produces P features f_p, p=1..P, and a transformer predicts C class embeddings, c_i, i=1..C. A grouping layer combines the spectrogram features f_p and class embeddings c_i to generate source embeddings g_n, n=1..N. I am not sure how source embeddings g_n are generated from class embeddings c_i; in some places, there are C source embeddings g, in other places there are N source embeddings. Using these class-aware source embeddings, a lightweight reconstruction layer generates N masks m_n, n=1..N for the input spectrogram.

To train this model, there is a grouping loss, which is 
$$
\sum_{i=1}^C CE(h_i, Softmax[ FC[ c_i ] ] )
+BCE(y_i, Sigmoid[ [FC[ g_i ]])
$$
where h_i is C-dimensional one-hot vector for class i, and y_i is binary label for class i in the training example. The CE loss promotes class embeddings c_i to be semantic, and the BCE loss is weak supervision using class label. There is also a reconstruction loss that is binary cross-entropy between ground-truth masks and estimates masks.

The approach is evaluated on MUSIC (11 classes) and FUSS () datasets, and is compared to multiple baselines with bss_eval SDR/SIR/SAR. The proposed method is shown to improve by about 0.4 dB SDR on MUSIC, and 0.7 dB SDR on FUSS.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths

1) Using class information can be a good way to boost separation performance, and it is useful to predict classes of separated sources. I think using transformers with these semantic embeddings has minor novelty.

Weaknesses

1) The description of the method is quite confusing, and I'm not quite sure I fully understand it, even after reading through it multiple times. Specific issues:

    **1a)** It's confusing that the class embeddings c_i, i=1..C and source embeddings g_i, i=1..N or i=1..C (both conventions are used) use the same index variable name i. I would recommend using a different index variable name for these, e.g. c_i, i=1..C and g_n, n=1..N, or if N is a subset of C, be specific and explicit about this in the notation. Even after reading the paper multiple times, I am confused how many g_i vectors there are. Is it C or N? Does N get chosen as a subset of C at test time?

    **1b)** For the CE loss, it seems that only the classes present in a training mixture can be used. So the notation should be adjusted to be something like C' \subset C to indicate this.

2) The paper ignores a lot of prior related work:

    **2a)** Fatemeh Pishdadian, Gordon Wichern, Jonathan Le Roux, "Finding Strength in Weakness: Learning to Separate Sounds with Weak Supervision," in IEEE/ACM Transactions on Audio, Speech, and Language Processing, Vol. 28, pp. 2386–2399, Sep. 2020 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.02182) also proposed using source class as a weak supervision signal, so this is not a novel proposal.

    **2b)** Seetharaman, Prem, Gordon Wichern, Shrikant Venkataramani, and Jonathan Le Roux. "Class-conditional embeddings for music source separation." In Proc. ICASSP 2019, pp. 301-305 (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1811.03076.pdf) proposed a deep clustering-based separation framework where the distribution of vectors in the embedding space are conditioned on an input source class. Since this is deep clustering, it also supports variable number of sources.

    **2c)** Tzinis, Efthymios, Scott Wisdom, John R. Hershey, Aren Jansen, and Daniel PW Ellis. "Improving universal sound separation using sound classification." In Proc. ICASSP 2020 pp. 96-100 (https://arxiv.org/abs/1911.07951) experimented with conditioning on classification predictions of a mixture, then iterating with conditioning on class predictions from preliminary sources.

    **2d)** Hershey, John R., Zhuo Chen, Jonathan Le Roux, and Shinji Watanabe. "Deep clustering: Discriminative embeddings for segmentation and separation." In Proc. ICASSP 2016, pp. 31-35 (https://arxiv.org/pdf/1508.04306.pdf). Deep clustering is a separation architecture that can handle variable number of sources by clustering per-time-frequency bin embeddings.

3) This is incorrect: 

    "MixIT (Wisdom et al., 2020) developed an unsupervised learning algorithm with permutation invariant training".

    MixIT does not use permutation-invariant training, in that it does not optimize over permutation matrices mapping N estimated sources to N references. Rather, it optimizes a 2xN matrix that maps N estimated sources to 2 reference mixtures.

4) This footnote:

    "1For past audio separation methods, a trained 2-sound separator will always produce 2 audio outputs. They cannot be used to handle mixtures with different number of sources."

    and this statement:

    "Different from previous sound separation approaches, the proposed SGN can support separation from a flexible number of sound sources"

    ignores prior work e.g. the FUSS paper, where a separation model can be trained with a _maximum_ number of sources M to separate mixtures with 1 to M sources, thus accomplishing variable number of sources. Also, these statements ignores deep clustering separation methods, where the number of sources is set by the number of clusters k at test time.

5) I don't understand how the FUSS dataset is evaluated. FUSS consists of mixtures of 1 to 4 sources, and care must be taken to account for this during evaluation. The original FUSS paper (https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.00803) defines separate metrics for single-source and multi-source mixtures. How is the evaluation done here? Is the SDR evaluated just for non-zero reference sources? And is the oracle number of sources used for each mixture? It would be better to use the evaluation procedure specified by the FUSS paper. Also, having used the FUSS dataset in the past, I don't think source classes are actually available. Did the authors figure out a way to get the source classes for mixtures? Please describe this if so.

6) It would be nice to include the network that extracts class tokens c_i in Figure 1.

7) How are audio waveforms reconstructed from masks and input spectrograms? Is the inverse STFT applied to the mask times the input complex STFT, i.e. using noisy phase? Please specify this.

8) In my experience, I have generally found signal-level losses to work better than mask-level losses for separation models.

9) This method relies on a lot of supervised labels: it can only be trained on synthetic mixtures of single sources, where the class labels are available for these individual sources. Given that such data is expensive and difficult to gather, I find this statement to be incorrect: "In addition, we do not need the unsupervised learning on large-scale simulated audio data with expensive training costs.". The training is not any more expensive than the proposed supervised method; the difference is that much more data can be used, e.g. given a large enough amount of unsupervised data (of which there is plenty), a model need never see the same example twice. In contrast, a network trained on the smaller amount of supervised data will have to see examples many times, limiting its possible generalization.

10) The paper claims

    "is capable of generalizing to tackle sources from different audio domains."

    but this is not shown. The approach is trained on matching data for MUSIC and FUSS, and I don't think there are any cross-evaluation experiments. Also, FUSS is limited in size, and does not necessarily generalize to real-world audio data (as shown in Table 1 of the MixIT paper https://arxiv.org/pdf/2006.12701.pdf, where MoMi score on real YFCC100M mixtures is nearly 0 for a model only trained on supervised FUSS)

11) None of the baseline methods use class information to condition on or for weak supervision. Thus, the proposed method is able to use additional information, and the existing baselines are strawmen. This would be somewhat if there were no other prior methods that don't condition on class information, but there are indeed multiple prior works that do use semantic information for conditioning (see weakness 2).
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Clarity

The paper is not very clear, especially in the description of the method, and important details about evaluation are excluded.

Quality

The description of the approach is rather confusing (see weaknesses above), and the paper makes many incorrect and unsupported claims. The paper does not cite or discuss a lot of related prior work. There are potential problems with evaluation (see weakness 5) and the baselines are not allowed to use semantic information, making them strawmen.

Novelty

Many prior works (not cited) have considered semantic conditioning for separation. Thus, the only novelty of this paper is the self-attention architecture for extracting and conditioning semantic embeddings, which is minor novelty.

Reproducibility

The paper claims that code and pre-trained models will be released on acceptance. The paper uses publicly available data (MUSIC and FUSS).
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper proposes a sound separation architecture that predicts and conditions on semantic information. Unfortunately, the paper is quite confusing in its description of the method, makes multiple unsupported claims, is missing references to a lot of prior related work, has potential issues with evaluation, and has limited novelty.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 1: The contributions are neither significant nor novel.

content.confidence: 4: You are confident in your assessment, but not absolutely certain. It is unlikely, but not impossible, that you did not understand some parts of the submission or that you are unfamiliar with some pieces of related work.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The authors propose to learn a basis set (called tokens) and a corresponding grouping function that combines these bases functions for separating the audio sources in a mixture. The paper is well presented and the technique is well motivated. The evaluations show promising results for the approach.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
The hypothesis that grouping clean sounds and adding some structured noise into this creates a mixture is a well motivated idea. Instead of starting with a real set of clean sounds, enabling an algorithm to learn this (tokens) is neat. 

Questions: 
1) From Table 3, can the authors comment on why the jump in performance is higher for SCT and no-CAG vs. CAG and no-SCT? Is this because the grouping representation is basically token representation + an additive term? Do you think a more non-linear operation here would have helped (albeit difficulty in training)? 
2) The visualizations in Fig 3 seems to indicate that the implicit variance in representations from a given class seems to be aggressively nullified in the proposed model compared to SoP. Can the authors comment on this further? Its important to maintain the natural variance of data for a given sound category. And how does this relate to question/comment 1) above. 
3) Can the authors comment about the robust ness of the model (especially the grouping) to noise in the data? In other words, are the 2 datasets noise free given that they are mainly music focused? Do we have examples where the weights/grouping fail due to strong broadband music/source like noise? 
4) What are the 10 classes from FUSS and how do the visualizations of tokens look like for that dataset? 
5) Is is fair to say that SoP with audio-visual is very similar to the proposal with audio-only, in other words, how much is a significant jump in performance for SIR and SAR compared to SDR and what does that tell us about the question 1) (i.e., the compactness of the resulting tokens killing the implicit variance in a given class and hence pushing the SIR and SDR to higher values)?
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
The clarity of the presentation is good. The related work is explained well. 
The evaluations are minimal in terms of exhaustiveness but they do capture the essence of the proposal. 
All the results are reproducible given the simplicity of the model.
content.summary_of_the_review: Although there is no major technical novelty in the paper (theoretical or mathematical), the proposed weighing procedure for the grouping seems to do a good job. The results are useful (but marginally) for the audio and sound source separation communities.
content.correctness: 4: All of the claims and statements are well-supported and correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper describes a method for audio source separation that tries to use labels (weak labels) of sound categories during training but not during inference.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. A method that uses categories of sounds.

Weaknesses:
1. Method is clearly behind state of the art.
2. Uses time-frequency embeddings which typically do not work better than direct prediction and classification models.
3. The method is not well described, for example how to reduce C entities to N entities.
4. The result on FUSS in Table 2 seems wrong. The SI-SNR number in the original Wisdom et.al. 2021 paper is 9.9 dB for 2-4 classes. Here the authors obtain an SDR of 3.93 which does not seem to correspond to the result in the original paper.
5. The paper does not mention how variable number of sources are handled in the model.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper has unclear parts such as how to reduce the C group probabilities into N source embeddings.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper describes a method that uses sound categories for separation. The method described seems behind state of the art since the model uses time-frequency embeddings to perform shallow classification and assignment. These approaches are superseded by deeper architectures in recent work.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
